prompt.context: Your client, Restoration Co., is a fire and water remediation company that specializes in extensive cleanup in the aftermath of fires and floods. They are currently hired by insurance companies on behalf of those affected by these disasters. While this existing business is quite profitable, they are looking to expand into the residential cleaning market (typical household cleaning, such as vacuuming, dusting, etc.). They have come to BCG with two questions: 1. What is the size of the residential cleaning market? 2. Should the company enter this market?
prompt.question: First, estimate the size of the US residential cleaning market. Then, assess whether Restoration Co. should enter this market.

clarifying_info.q: Which geography are we looking at?
clarifying_info.a: The client is only looking at the US right now (all of it).

clarifying_info.q: How many households are in the US?
clarifying_info.a: There are 100MM households in the US.
The US residential cleaning market is growing steadily with inflation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's primary goal?
clarifying_info.a: Their main goal is to enter the market profitably.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average price for a single cleaning service?
clarifying_info.a: Average price for a cleaning service is $75.

clarifying_info.q: How long does an average cleaning take?
What are the supply costs per job?
What is the typical annual spend per household on cleaning services?

exhibits.title: Market Sizing – Willingness to Pay by Income Segment
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the 100MM US households segmented by household income relative to $75,000, with willingness-to-pay percentages for each income segment
exhibits.data: 100MM total households; split 50/50 above and below $75K income; above $75K: 40% WTP; below $75K: 10% WTP

exhibits.title: Competitive Landscape – Market Share by Player Type
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the residential cleaning market by competitor type showing their share of the market and how each type competes
exhibits.data: National players: 10% of market, compete on quality; Regional players: 20% of market, compete on both quality and price; Individual players: 70% of market, compete on price

exhibits.title: Unit Economics – Revenue, Cost, and Profit per Cleaning Job
exhibits.shows: Revenue, cost components, and profit figures for a single residential cleaning job at the national player pricing level
exhibits.data: Revenue: $75 per job; Labor cost: $10/hour x 5 hours = $50; Supply cost: $5 per job; Total cost: $55; Profit: $20

framework: Market sizing: estimate total addressable market using household count, income segmentation, and willingness to pay, then apply annual spend
Market entry assessment: analyze competitive landscape (players, positioning, market share)
Positioning: determine where Restoration Co. should compete on the quality-price spectrum based on brand fit
Profitability: calculate unit economics (revenue, cost, margin) for the target segment
Differentiation: identify ways to separate Restoration Co. from competitors
Recommendation: synthesize findings into go/no-go with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: How would you segment the 100MM US households to estimate the number of households willing to pay for cleaning services?
questions.guidance: Candidate should arrive at segmentation by socioeconomic status / household income. Geography and home type are acceptable ideas but the key segmentation is income above vs. below $75K. Candidate should recognize that higher-income households have higher willingness to pay. Split: 50MM households above $75K (40% WTP) and 50MM below $75K (10% WTP).

math.setup: 100MM households split 50/50 by income at $75K threshold. WTP rates: above $75K = 40%, below $75K = 10%.
steps: Above $75K: 50MM x 40% = 20MM households willing to pay
Below $75K: 50MM x 10% = 5MM households willing to pay
math.answer: 25MM households purchase cleaning services per year

questions.prompt: Given 25MM purchasing households, what is the total market size in dollars?
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for (or recall) the average annual spend per household. 25MM purchases is not the market size — it must be converted to revenue. If the interviewer says 'That's a pretty big number' after the candidate gives $50B, look for confidence; candidate should stand behind the math.

math.setup: 25MM purchasing households x $2,000 average annual spend per household

questions.prompt: How would you go about figuring out whether Restoration Co. should enter the market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about the competitive landscape. Key dimensions: player types, their market share, and how each competes (quality vs. price). National players (10%, quality), regional players (20%, both), individual players (70%, price).

questions.prompt: Where should Restoration Co. position itself on the quality-price spectrum?
questions.guidance: Candidate should argue for competing on quality. Supporting reasons: (1) Restoration Co. already does extensive high-quality cleanup after disasters, so quality cleaning is within its competency; (2) it should not dilute its brand by competing on price; (3) entering a price war against 70% of the market (highly fragmented individuals) is unattractive. Bonus: candidate should note that competing only with national players reduces the addressable market from $50B to $5B (10% of $50B).

math.setup: Addressable market if competing at quality tier = national players' share of total market

questions.prompt: How would you figure out the profitability of competing as a national-tier quality player?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build unit economics from the given data: revenue per job ($75), labor cost ($10/hr x 5 hrs = $50), supplies ($5/job), total cost ($55), profit ($20). Candidate should then compute profit margin and interpret it.

math.setup: Revenue per job = $75; Labor = $10/hr x 5 hrs; Supplies = $5/job

questions.prompt: What else should Restoration Co. consider before entering the market, and how can it differentiate from competition?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm differentiation levers. Strong ideas: using premium/sustainable cleaning supplies; performing a home safety survey to assess fire or flood hazards (natural extension of core business); offering a free first cleaning to acquire customers. Weak idea: entering a pricing war in a quality-focused segment.

brainstorming.prompt: How can Restoration Co. differentiate itself from other national-tier residential cleaning competitors?

categories.name: Product/Service enhancements
ideas: Use premium or sustainable cleaning chemicals
Use scented shampoo and high-end supplies to signal quality

categories.name: Leveraging core competency
ideas: Perform a complimentary home survey to assess fire or flood hazard risks — natural extension of existing business
Bundle cleaning with hazard inspection as a unique value-add

categories.name: Customer acquisition
ideas: Offer a free first cleaning to reduce trial friction
Leverage existing insurance-company client relationships to refer homeowners

categories.name: Brand positioning
ideas: Position as a premium, trust-based brand (safety + cleanliness)
Avoid any pricing promotions that dilute quality positioning

recommendation: Restoration Co. should enter the residential cleaning market. The total market is $50B; competing at the quality tier alongside national players addresses a $5B segment. Unit economics are attractive at a 27% profit margin, and the company's existing disaster-cleanup expertise provides a credible quality narrative.
risks: 27% margin needs to be benchmarked against Restoration Co.'s current business margins to assess relative attractiveness
Possible brand dilution if the residential cleaning offering is perceived as lower-quality than the remediation business — mitigated by committing to premium products and positioning
Entering a fragmented price-competitive segment (70% of market) would be a mistake; must remain disciplined to quality tier
next_steps: Review financing requirements and up-front capital costs (equipment, hiring, training)
Determine how to leverage existing insurance-company client book to generate initial residential referrals
Redesign the sales model — current model relies on insurance company B2B relationships; residential market requires direct-to-consumer or door-to-door marketing
Define a differentiated service offering (e.g., safety survey + premium supplies) before launch
